answer: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a serious condition associated with significant health risks. It increases the risk of stroke and mortality, and can greatly limit quality of life [1]. The lifetime risk of AF is high, with approximately 24% at age 40, and this risk remains fairly constant at older ages, with 22% at age 80 [1]. AF is responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality, with the risk of stroke increasing from 1.5% in patients aged 50-59 years to up to 23.5% for those aged 80-89 years [4]. The absolute risk of in-hospital medical complications is higher in patients with AF, at 43.3% compared to 24.4% in those without AF [3]. AF is a growing epidemic, with the number of cases expected to double in the U.S. and Europe by 2050 [1][4]. Its management is complex, involving risk stratification, prevention of thromboembolic complications, and decisions on rhythm versus rate control [5][7].
